newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ahern pledges minority Irish government will last.
newsitem.headline: Ahern pledges minority Irish government will last.

text.p: Ireland's Fianna Fail party leader Bertie Ahern, narrow winner of a cliffhanger general election at the weekend, on Monday brushed aside speculation of early, fresh polls and said he was determined his minority government would last its term.

"The aim will be to have a four or five year government," Ahern told Irish radio as he prepared to carry out campaign priorities to cut taxes, crime and boost the peace process in the violence-plagued, British-ruled province of Northern Ireland.

Ahern, whose centre-right alliance with the Progressive Democrats won 81 of parliament's 166 seats, said he hoped independent parties, on whose support he will have to rely, would be mindful of the need for political stability.
"I would hope most of them would be concerned about how long the new parliament can last. We have to get an arrangement that will last in the longer term," he said.

Ahern expects sympathisers among the seven independents elected would back his government programme in return for support for their local agenda, such as rural road-building and other development, political sources said.
Financial markets took the election of a minority government in their stride. They said the absence of a majority in parliament was mildly negative but foresaw no drastic change of economic course.
"The outcome of the election is marginally negative but we are seeing a muted reaction to it in the markets," Riada stockbroker economist Padhraic Garvey said.
"Currency movements are broadly ignoring the election result," AIB Capital Markets economist Pat O'Sullivan said.

Ahern will be formally voted in as prime minister when parliament reconvenes on June 26. The vanquished centre-left "Rainbow Coalition" of Prime Minister John Bruton will form a caretaker administration until then.

Outgoing Finance Minister Ruair Quinn told Reuters Financial Television in Luxembourg he hoped the new government would maintain Ireland's economic boom and was confident it would give the same backing to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"I hope that they will maintain the progress we have put in place and I would be reasonably confident that by and large they will," he said, while attending an EU Finance Ministers meeting.
"The commitment of the Irish government to the single currency project -- the incoming government -- will be the same as the outgoing government," Quinn said.

Ahern's plans to make former prime minister Albert Reynolds a key player in his efforts to rebuild the Northern Ireland peace process were mocked by a leading member of the province's pro-British Unionist community.

Ken Maginnis, security spokesman of the Ulster Unionist Party, the province's biggest political group, said Reynolds, who helped broker a 1994 truce by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) in its war against British rule in Northern Ireland, was a discredited politician.
Reynolds was forced to step down in 1994 in a row over top legal appointments with his Labour party allies.
The IRA broke their truce in February 1996 with a bomb in London which killed two people.
"For Bertie Ahern to suggest that he's going to foist some sort of recycled and discredited politician on the Northern Ireland scene is not going to be helpful," he said.

Unionists believe Reynolds promised the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, a deal under which it would gain immediate entry to current multi-party peace talks if the IRA called a new, definitive ceasefire.
The Irish and British governments have insisted that Sinn Fein remain barred from the talks while its guerrilla allies continue their campaign of violence.
